```{r}

# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(here)
library(stars)
library(tmap)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(knitr)
library(gt)
```

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# read in geodatabase of EJ Screen data 
ejscreen <- st_read(here::here("data-3", "ejscreen","EJSCREEN_2023_BG_StatePct_with_AS_CNMI_GU_VI.gdb"))

# filter LA County
los_angeles <- ejscreen %>%
    dplyr::filter(CNTY_NAME %in% c("Los Angeles County"))

# read in HOLC redlining data (change crs to match EJ Screen)
holc <- st_read(here::here("data-3", "mapping-inequality", "mapping-inequality-los-angeles.json")) |>
    st_transform(3857)

# read in bike and pedestiran crash reports (change crs to match EJ Screen)
crash_data <- read_csv(here::here("data-3", "SWITRS_LA", "Crashes.csv")) |>
    as_tibble() |> 
    drop_na(POINT_X) |> 
    drop_na(POINT_Y) |>  # Remove NAs from x and y columns
    st_as_sf(coords = c("POINT_X", "POINT_Y"), crs = 4326) |> 
    #Create a geometry with x and y
    st_transform(st_crs(holc))
```

```{r}
# Check CRS type of datasets to make sure they match
st_crs(ejscreen)
st_crs(los_angeles)
st_crs(holc)
st_crs(crash_data)
```


# Part 1: Legacy of redlining in current environmental (in)justice

## 1. Create a map of historical redlining neighborhoods, including:
- neighborhoods colored by HOLC grade
- an appropriate base map
- a clear title and legend

```{r}
tm_basemap("OpenStreetMap") +
tm_shape(holc) +
    tm_polygons(fill = 'grade', 
    fill.scale = tm_scale(values = c("forestgreen", "lightblue", "gold", "pink", "white")),
    fill.legend = tm_legend( title = "HOLC Grade")) +
    tm_scalebar() +
    tm_compass() +
    tm_layout(
      main.title = "Historical Redlining Neighborhoods",
      main.title.size = 1.1,
      legend.outside = TRUE
    )   
```

## 2. Create a table summarizing: 
```{r}
# Join datasets
joined <- st_join(los_angeles, holc) |> 
    st_drop_geometry()

# Create table that includes % of Census Block Groups within each HOLC grade
summary_table <- joined |> 
    count(grade) |> 
    mutate(Percentage = (n / nrow(los_angeles)*100)) |> 
    select(!n) |> 
    gt() |> 
    tab_header('% of Census Block Groups within each HOLC grade')

summary_table
```

Create two visualizations summarizing current conditions (from EJScreen data) within HOLC grades using the mean of the following variables:
- % low income
- percentile for PM 2.5
- percentile for low life expectancy
- use ggplot for visuals!

```{r}
# % low income
mean_percent_low_income <- joined |> 
  group_by(grade) |> 
  summarise(mean_percent_low_income = mean(LOWINCPCT)) |> 
  drop_na()

# percentile for PM 2.5
mean_percentile_PM25 <- joined |> 
  group_by(grade) |> 
  summarise(mean_percentile_PM25 = mean(P_PM25)) |> 
  drop_na()

# percentile for low life expectancy
mean_low_life_expectancty <- joined |> 
  group_by(grade) |> 
  summarise(mean_low_life_expectancty = mean(P_LIFEEXPPCT, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  drop_na()

```

## 3. Create at least two visualizations summarizing current conditions from EJScreen data within HOLC grades
```{r}
# Create a dictionary for colors
colors <- c(
    "A" = "forestgreen",
    "B" = "skyblue",
    "C" = "gold",
    "D" = "pink"
)

# Plot Mean Percent Low Income
ggplot(mean_percent_low_income, aes(grade, mean_percent_low_income, fill = grade)) +
    geom_col() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colors) +
    labs(
        title = "Mean Percentage of Low-Income Households by HOLC Grade",
        x = " HOLC Grade",
        y = "Mean Low-Income Population (%)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

# Plot Mean Percentile for PM 2.5
ggplot(mean_percentile_PM25, aes(grade, mean_percentile_PM25, fill = grade)) +
    geom_col() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colors) +
    labs(
        title = "Mean Percentile of Particulate Matter (PM2.5) by HOLC Grade",
        x = " HOLC Grade",
        y = "Mean Percentile of PM2.5"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

# Plot Mean Percentile for Low Life Expectancy
ggplot(mean_low_life_expectancty, aes(grade, mean_low_life_expectancty, fill = grade)) +
    geom_col() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colors) +
    labs(
        title = "Mean Low Life Expectancy Percentile by HOLC Grade",
        x = " HOLC Grade",
        y = "Mean Perecentile for Low Life Expectancy"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

```

# 4. Write a brief paragraph reflecting on these results
Interpret the patterns you observe in the results and discuss potential relationships between historical redlining grades and current environmental/socioeconomic conditions.

_The three ggplots reveal similar patterns between historical HOLC grades and present-day environmental and socioeconomic conditions in Los Angeles._

_The first plot, “Mean Percentage of Low-Income Households by HOLC Grade,” shows that neighborhoods historically assigned A or B grades have a lower mean percentage of low-income households compared to neighborhoods assigned C or D grades. Neighborhoods that received a D grade have the highest percentage of low-income households, at approximately 40%._

_A similar pattern appears in the second plot, “Mean Percentile of PM2.5 by HOLC Grade.” Neighborhoods historically assigned A or B grades have lower mean PM2.5 percentiles, while those assigned C or D grades have higher percentiles. Neighborhoods with a D grade have the highest mean PM2.5 percentile, at approximately 80%, suggesting greater exposure to fine particulate matter pollution._

_Finally, the third plot examining low life expectancy shows that neighborhoods assigned A or B grades have lower mean low-life-expectancy indicator values, suggesting more favorable life expectancy outcomes. In contrast, neighborhoods assigned C or D grades have higher values, with D-graded neighborhoods exceeding 50._

_Overall, these results suggest a relationship between historical redlining practices and present-day environmental and socioeconomic inequalities. Neighborhoods that were historically considered less desirable for investment continue to experience higher rates of low-income households, greater air pollution burdens, and less favorable life expectancy outcomes. These patterns highlight how historical discriminatory housing policies may have contributed to inequalities that persist today._

## Part 2: Legacy of redlining in pedestrian and bike accidents
1. A figure summarizing the percent of observations within redlines neighborhoods within each HOLC grade.

```{r}
# Check to make sure we have matching CRS'!
if(st_crs(crash_data) == st_crs(holc)){
  print("crs matches!")
}else{
  warning("crs does not match")
  print(paste("crash_data has", st_crs(crash_data), "crs")) 
  
  print(paste("holc has", st_crs(holc), "crs"))
  }
```

```{r}
# Filter for bike and pedestrian crashes
filtered_crashes <- crash_data |> 
    filter(PEDESTRIAN_ACCIDENT == 'Y' | BICYCLE_ACCIDENT == 'Y')
```

```{r}
crashes_la <- st_filter(filtered_crashes, los_angeles) # ensures everything in filtered_crashes is located in los angeles dataframe
```

```{r}
# Perform a spatial join
new_join <- st_join(crashes_la, holc) |> 
    st_drop_geometry()
```

```{r}
# Check range of observations (2020 - 2025)
min(new_join$ACCIDENT_YEAR)

max(new_join$ACCIDENT_YEAR)
```

```{r}
# Create table that includes % bike and pedestrian crashes and fatalities within each HOLC grade
new_table <- new_join |> 
    filter(!is.na(grade)) |> 
    group_by(grade) |> 
    summarize(n = n()) |> 
    mutate(Percentage = (n / nrow(new_join)*100))

new_table |>
    gt()|>
    tab_header('% of bike and pedestrian crashes and fatalities within each HOLC grade')

```
```{r}
# Plot percentage of bike and pedestrian crashes and fatalities within each HOLC grade
ggplot(new_table, aes(grade, Percentage, fill = grade)) +
    geom_col() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colors) +
    labs(
        title = "Share of Bike and Pedestrian Crashes by HOLC Grade (LA County, 2020 - 2025)",
        x = "HOLC Grade",
        y = "Share of All Crashes (%)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
```

# Part 2 Plot Analysis
_The plot shows the share of bike and pedestrian crashes in Los Angeles County (2020 - 2025) that occurred within each HOLC grade. Grade C neighborhoods account for the largest share at roughly 27%, followed by grade D at about 13%, grade B at about 5%, and grade A at about 1%. The two lower-graded categories (C and D) together contain over 40% of crashes, while the higher-graded categoeries (A and B) contain only about 6%. This suggests that crashes are conentrated in historically disinvested neighborhoods, which fits the Part 1 results and research linking redlined areas to worse pedestrian safety outcomes._
